clue.text: Burst from trumpeter? One can't go as high as Armstrong did

definitions.text: One can't go as high as Armstrong did

parts.note: an elephant trumpets, and Jumbo is the classic elephant name
a jet is a sudden burst of liquid or gas

explanation.surface: A jazz trumpeter blasts out a note, while somebody muses about Louis Armstrong's soaring high notes.
explanation.walkthrough: Armstrong looks like Louis the trumpeter, which the surface encourages; the definition means Neil Armstrong, who reached the moon.
explanation.definitionFit: An airliner flies high but never reaches the moon, where astronaut Neil Armstrong walked in 1969.

clue.text: Regular servings of bug food for a drone, probably?

indicators.note: servings at regular intervals means taking every other letter of the words that follow

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Someone feeds an insect at regular mealtimes, wondering whether a drone bee would eat it.
explanation.walkthrough: A drone looks like a male bee, fitting the bug food; it is really the flying gadget often reported as a mystery object in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Many sightings of unidentified flying objects turn out, on inspection, to be remote-controlled flying machines.

clue.text: See 26 Across
Black-coloured stocking is lost

parts.note: jet is a deep black colour

indicators.note: stocking here means holding inside, as a shop stocks goods, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: toned can mean tinted or coloured
taken as written

explanation.surface: A black stocking has gone missing from the drawer.
explanation.walkthrough: Stocking looks like hosiery, matching black, but it is a verb: one piece holds another the way a shop holds stock.
explanation.definitionFit: Cargo thrown overboard is discarded and gone, so jettisoned works as a past participle meaning got rid of.

clue.text: Teensy bit squiffy

definitions.meaning: first meaning: very small, a British informal word
second meaning: slightly drunk; squiffy is British slang for tipsy

explanation.surface: A tiny bit tipsy after a drink or two.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses are British informal words: one means tiny, the other mildly drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: The British colloquial adjective means both very little and slightly intoxicated after a modest amount of alcohol.

clue.text: See 21
House of dance

parts.note: HO is the standard abbreviation for house
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dance company or venue, the House of Dance.
explanation.walkthrough: House of Dance looks like a name; it is the abbreviation HO, the word OF, then the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To hoof it is informal slang for dancing, especially tap or chorus-line stepping on stage.

clue.text: Shame about leader in fanzine penned by hack, say — filthy language

indicators.note: something penned by another is shut up inside it, like an animal in a pen

parts.note: as in 'what a shame', 'what a pity'

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the first word wraps round what follows

parts.note: a hack is a riding horse, and a roan is a horse of mixed colouring; 'say' marks the example

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: its opening letter

explanation.surface: It's a shame a hack journalist wrote a piece in a fanzine full of swearing.
explanation.walkthrough: Hack looks like a journalist, which suits the fanzine, but it is a horse; a roan is one with a coat of mixed colours.
explanation.definitionFit: Profanity is swearing or obscene speech, the kind of foul talk the clue calls filthy.

clue.text: Enlightenment in rebranding of Labour Party post-David Miliband?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: moral or intellectual improvement

definitions.text: rebranding of Labour Party post-David Miliband
definitions.meaning: second, punning meaning: making the party Ed's, since Ed Miliband beat his brother David to the leadership in 2010

explanation.surface: A political commentator asks what lesson the Labour Party learned after David Miliband lost out.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as ED-IFICATION, the word becomes the process of turning something into Ed: Ed Miliband beat his brother David for the Labour leadership in 2010.
explanation.definitionFit: Edification is instruction that improves the mind or morals, a close synonym for enlightenment.

clue.text: Vessel for wine in tiny mouth?

parts.note: gob is British slang for mouth
-let is a suffix that makes things small, as in piglet

explanation.surface: Someone pours wine into a baby's little mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the other way, a tiny mouth is a mouth-let: GOB with the diminutive ending LET.
explanation.definitionFit: A goblet is a drinking cup with a stem and foot, traditionally used for serving wine.

clue.text: Tennis player for whom Covid jabs originally OK? That's unlikely

indicators.note: something unlikely is improbable or out of order, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: originally points to the start of a word, so just its opening letter is used

parts.note: its opening letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tennis star who said no to vaccinations is asked whether jabs are OK: unlikely.
explanation.walkthrough: Novak Djokovic famously refused the Covid vaccine and was deported from Australia in 2022, so the surface fits him exactly.
explanation.definitionFit: Novak Djokovic is the Serbian player who has won a record number of Grand Slam singles titles.

clue.text: Mouthpiece, glue's stuck around one

parts.note: gum is a glue, and the 's is kept as S

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the preceding word wraps round the next item

parts.note: held fast, stuck in place
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A mouthpiece won't stay put because the glue has stuck around it.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in glue's is kept as an S. A gumshield is the guard boxers bite on, so mouthpiece is literal, not a spokesperson.
explanation.definitionFit: A gumshield is the protective guard a boxer or rugby player wears over the teeth.

clue.text: Composed, as are rigid wings?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: calm, never getting agitated
second, playful meaning: wings that cannot flap

explanation.surface: Someone notes how calm a stiff-winged glider appears.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as UN-FLAP-PABLE: stiff wings are literally not able to flap.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone unflappable stays calm under pressure, keeping cool and collected whatever happens.

clue.text: Prestidigitation, smoke and mirrors initially given reflection?

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror shows things back to front, so the whole string is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: a cig is a cigarette, a smoke

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each of the words takes only its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A conjuror's trick is all smoke and mirrors, with a reflection thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: Smoke and mirrors looks like one phrase meaning illusion, but it is split: CIG, then A and M, all reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Prestidigitation is sleight of hand, the conjuring skill of a stage magician.

clue.text: Skeletal structure in Facebook address of Paul?

parts.note: Meta is the company that owns Facebook
St Paul was Saul of Tarsus, his home town

explanation.surface: Someone looks up the Facebook address of a man named Paul.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul is also the setter's name, so the clue winks at him; the address is the apostle's home town.
explanation.definitionFit: The metatarsus is the group of five long bones in the foot between the ankle and the toes.

clue.text: Anything but a real swine cradling head of love bird

indicators.note: cradling means holding within the arms, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: facon is fake bacon, a vegetarian imitation, so anything but real pig meat

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: its first letter

explanation.surface: A lovebird is anything but a real pig.
explanation.walkthrough: Facon is a portmanteau of fake and bacon: plant-based rashers. L goes inside it after FA.
explanation.definitionFit: The falcon is a fast hawk-like bird of prey, famous for its high-speed hunting dives.

clue.text: Sinking ship proceeds to capsize, with rat running around

indicators.note: running around means encircling, so one word wraps round the other

parts.note: a rat and a louse are both contemptible people

indicators.note: a capsized boat is turned upside down, so in a down entry the word is flipped end to end

parts.note: the verb: proceeds, acts, takes action

explanation.surface: A sinking ship starts to capsize while the rats scurry about the deck.
explanation.walkthrough: Proceeds looks like a noun for money but is the verb ACTS, turned to STCA and wrapped by LOUSE: LO-STCA-USE.
explanation.definitionFit: Figuratively a sinking ship is an enterprise doomed to fail, which is exactly a hopeless cause.

clue.text: Sovereign a nation recalled

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the words are taken backwards

parts.note: taken as written
Niger is a West African nation

explanation.surface: A monarch's country has called back its ambassador.
explanation.definitionFit: Regina is Latin for queen, used of the reigning female monarch, as in the royal cipher ER.

clue.text: Parting shot from spinning of S. Warne

indicators.note: spinning sends things whirling, so the letters are turned into a new order; Shane Warne was a famous spin bowler

parts.note: the initial and surname of the Australian cricketer

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator describes Shane Warne's final ball as a parting shot.
explanation.walkthrough: Shane Warne was an Australian leg-spin bowler, so spinning sounds like his cricket, not a letter shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A reply or retort fired back as the last word in an exchange works as a parting shot.

clue.text: Old documents reviewing pay in middle of April

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so one piece goes within the other
re-viewing suggests looking again in a new way, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: these three letters rearranged

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letters, dropping the ends

parts.note: the month without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: An accountant goes over old pay records in mid-April, at the start of the tax year.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the tax year begins in early April, which suits the reviewing of pay.
explanation.definitionFit: Papyri are ancient manuscripts written on sheets made from the papyrus reed, the plural of papyrus.

clue.text: Black sheep spoiled food on farm?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a disreputable member of a family or group
second meaning, literally: a rotten one laid by a hen

explanation.surface: A dark sheep tramples food on a farm.
explanation.walkthrough: Black sheep looks like farm livestock, matching the farm food, but it is the idiom for a rogue.
explanation.definitionFit: Both idioms describe a person of bad character who brings shame on the group they belong to.

clue.text: Bouncer with velocity punching customer

indicators.note: punching drives into something, so one word is pushed inside the other

parts.note: a customer in a shop
pace is speed

explanation.surface: A nightclub bouncer swiftly punches a customer.
explanation.walkthrough: A bouncer looks like a doorman, but here it is a toy: a space hopper is a large inflatable ball with handles that children sit on and bounce around.
explanation.definitionFit: A space hopper is a rubber ball with horns to grip, ridden by bouncing along on it.

clue.text: Syrian mother has a tantrum

parts.note: a dam is an animal's mother
taken as written
to make a scene is to throw a tantrum

explanation.surface: A Syrian mother loses her temper.
explanation.definitionFit: Damascene describes something from Damascus, the capital of Syria.

clue.text: African carrier, first of containers, A, B or C?

indicators.note: first of points to the opening letter of the word that follows

parts.note: its first letter
taken as written
Mel B and Mel C were both Spice Girls, so either is a Mel

explanation.surface: A shipping firm in Africa labels its containers A, B or C.
explanation.walkthrough: A, B or C reads like a list of labels, but B or C finishes the names Mel B and Mel C, two of the Spice Girls pop group.
explanation.definitionFit: Camels carry goods and people across the Sahara and other African deserts as pack animals.

clue.text: Fine wine?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: French ça va, 'it's going well', sounds the same
second meaning: a Spanish sparkling white

explanation.walkthrough: Fine wine looks like one phrase for a classy bottle; the first word stands alone as the French reply ça va, meaning fine.
explanation.definitionFit: Cava is sparkling Spanish wine, and ça va is the everyday French for I'm fine.

clue.text: Hard bread out at sea

indicators.note: at sea means confused and all over the place, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the letters of these two words together

explanation.surface: A sailor finds the bread has gone hard on a long voyage.
explanation.definitionFit: Obdurate means stubbornly unyielding, hard-hearted and resistant to persuasion.

clue.text: Gymnast: be lissome in twists

indicators.note: twists means contorts out of shape, so the letters are bent into a new order

parts.note: the letters of these three words together

explanation.surface: Advice to a gymnast: stay supple as you twist.
explanation.walkthrough: In looks like a link word but is part of the letters; twists suits a gymnast doing her routine.
explanation.definitionFit: Simone Biles is the American gymnast with the most world and Olympic medals in the sport.

clue.text: Celibate, with some frustration, understandably

indicators.note: some means a portion, so the letters are a part of the following words

parts.note: running across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: Someone who has taken a vow of chastity may feel frustrated, understandably.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman in a religious order takes a vow of chastity, so a celibate can be one.

clue.text: Franco's money put into plant

indicators.note: into means placed inside, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: a pea is a plant
to put something down is to set it

explanation.surface: A dictator's cash is invested in a factory.
explanation.walkthrough: Plant looks like a factory; it is the vegetable. General Franco ruled Spain, and the peseta was the Spanish currency before the euro.
explanation.definitionFit: The peseta was the money of Spain, under Franco and until the euro arrived in 2002.

clue.text: Fuel like crude oil in engine not half backfiring!

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the first part sits within the second
backfiring means going off backwards, so the letters run in the other direction
not half means half of the word is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
like and as both mean in the manner of

indicators.note: crude means unrefined and rough, so the word after it is in a raw, rearranged state

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A mechanic complains that the engine is backfiring on crude fuel.
explanation.walkthrough: Crude oil looks like one phrase but crude acts only on the second word. Gasoline is the American term; British readers say petrol.
explanation.definitionFit: Gasoline is the refined liquid fuel that powers most car engines, called petrol in Britain.
